candidate_sources.title: Petal Blight of Camellia
candidate_sources.snippet: Petal blight symptoms begin within 48 hours of infection as small brownish specks with an uneven margin. Spots enlarge and eventually cover the whole petal; the whole flower becomes brown. The fungus invades to the flower base where a hard, black sclerotium forms. Sclerotia produce apothecia that release windblown ascospores.

candidate_sources.title: Camellia Petal Blight / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms distinguishing camellia petal blight include petal veins darker than surrounding tissue giving a netted appearance, infections beginning near the central part of the flower, and symptoms only on petals. Diagnosed by a ring of white or gray mycelium at the base of the petals after removal of the calyx. Sanitation is the most effective management strategy.

candidate_sources.title: Camellia-Flower and Petal Blight | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Hard brown-to-black sclerotia develop in the base of old infected flowers and produce mushroom-like apothecia, which release spores that cause new petal infections. Sclerotia can survive in soil at least 4 years. Spores are windblown and can travel up to 1 mile. Rake and destroy infected flowers and debris.

candidate_sources.title: Camellia Diseases and Insect Pests in South Carolina | Home & Garden Information Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Camellia flower blight is caused by the fungus Ciborinia camelliae, which infects flowers causing them to turn brown, mushy, and fall off. Small brown spots on petals enlarge until the whole flower becomes brown. Sanitation: remove and destroy diseased flowers and the top 3 to 4 inches of soil from beneath plants to eliminate sclerotia.
